prompt:
Turn each research decision below into a neutral multiple-choice item. For each you get a context and several options in random order; the team took exactly one of them and you are not told which. Do not try to work out which.

For each item return:
- "context": the context rewritten in neutral third person (2-5 sentences). Keep its facts. Remove anything that favours one option or hints at what was done or learned later. Do not name any person, lab, organisation or paper, and do not use a coined name for the phenomenon; describe it in plain words.
- "question": one short line naming the decision, e.g. "Which evaluation should the team build?"
- "options": every option restated, keyed by its label, in ONE fixed form: exactly one sentence; imperative, present tense ("Run ...", "Frame ..."); no first person (we, our, us, I, my, me); no hedges; no digits (write numbers as words only if every option carries the same kind of number); no names. Keep each option's meaning and its key specifics, at the same level of detail across options. All options of an item must have nearly the same length: every option between 155 and 185 characters. Do not make any option sound more careful, more expert or more polished than the others.

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "context": str, "question": str, "options": {"<label>": str}}]}

ITEMS:

=== key 1aae4b3b1326
Context: The team was studying whether language models give practical, hard-to-verify advice that is quietly shaped by the model's own values, and whether the model tells the user when that happens. They needed a concrete phenomenon and a way to demonstrate it. One candidate scenario has a user deciding whether to invest in an AI company and asking how likely an AI bubble is to pop, with the company varied between the model's own developer and a competitor.
O1: Mine real user conversations for naturally occurring advice requests where the model's values could plausibly matter, and build matched decoy and baseline items, so any claim rests on a natural distribution and is treated as an existence proof.
O2: Study value influence as a basic property of how models form beliefs, using abstract probes such as preference elicitation and internal-representation analysis, without tying the work to a particular user decision scenario or a claim about user harm.
O3: Chose to study covert value leakage, meaning whether answers are shaped by the model's own values and whether the model discloses this. They built a suite of evaluations, including a scenario where a user weighs investing in an AI company and asks how likely an AI bubble is to pop.
O4: Study the phenomenon by comparing behaviour with and without cues about the model's perceived oversight or evaluation status, treating the model's stated belief that it is being tested as data, to see whether the value influence is conditional on being watched.
O5: Compare stated and expressed value preferences by putting models in forced-choice scenarios that trade off values against each other, rather than studying undisclosed influence on user advice.

=== key e1f397ca21f6
Context: The team needed evidence both that a model's answers shift because of its values and that the model fails to tell the user about this. They had candidate tasks such as investment-risk estimates where the company under consideration is varied, and a Fermi-estimation task where the model produces reasoning before answering. The measurement had to separate the size of the answer shift from whether the stated reasoning or answer acknowledges it.
O1: Add a causal intervention: edit or resample the reasoning trace, e.g. insert or remove value-related statements, and see whether answers change, to establish what the model is actually responding to.
O2: Built evaluations that quantify both the shift in answers and the disclosure. The abstract suggests this includes reading the chain-of-thought on a Fermi-estimation task and comparing answers across contexts, such as Anthropic vs OpenAI as the company under consideration.
O3: Run a rule-based quantitative comparison, such as scoring numeric answers with a proper scoring metric, across a fixed validation set and many models, instead of reading free-text reasoning for disclosure.
O4: Hand-grade a small set of transcripts for disclosure with explicit rubric criteria and report counts, rather than relying on automated quantification across many items.
O5: Include blind and ablated baselines, with the value-relevant cue removed and with borderline decoy contexts where no influence is expected, so that shifts in answers can be attributed to the intended value rather than to incidental differences between prompts.

=== key 345ccc39500a
Context: Having seen value-driven answer shifts in one scenario involving a company preference, the team had to decide how far to extend the study. Value leakage might be a quirk of one type of value or one model family. Candidate extensions covered moral preferences, loyalty to the developer, and preferences among human leisure activities, across several frontier models.
O1: Narrow to a single value, such as developer loyalty, and characterise it in depth, including its triggers, size and dependence on prompt details, in one or two models.
O2: Tested several types of values: moral preferences, loyalty to the developer company, and preferences among human leisure activities. They also compared multiple frontier models, including Claude and Qwen.
O3: Fix one value type and one scenario family in advance, build many equivalent variants with irrelevant details varied, and run matched baselines, so a robust and narrowly scoped claim is established before generalising.
O4: Use a broad survey-style set of value dimensions and compare many models on forced-choice scenarios, reporting differences across value categories.
O5: Run a single well-validated value type across many models with blind and ablated controls, and treat the outcome as an existence proof per model rather than a cross-value generality claim.

=== key be66b7a7a6d7
Context: The team had found that answers shift with the model's values and that the model often does not disclose this, with large differences among models. They had to decide how to categorise this failure and how strongly to state it. Related failure modes exist that it superficially resembles, and the disclosure rate for one model was high but not universal.
O1: Make a narrow claim that these particular evaluations show answer shifts and low disclosure for the tested models, leaving the question of misalignment classification and adequacy of current training to future work.
O2: Characterise the behaviour on the overt versus covert dimension, describing it as a covert form of misalignment where the surface output looks fine while the underlying influence is hidden, rather than as a wholly separate failure mode.
O3: Frame it as a narrowly scoped, caveated finding about these specific setups, noting that the scenarios may exaggerate incentives and making no claim about prevalence or about adequacy of existing training.
O4: Called covert value leakage a form of misalignment and said it is distinct from sycophancy and reward hacking. They said current alignment training and evaluations do not adequately address it. They used a hedged phrasing for the Claude result ('mostly fails to disclose').
O5: Present the results as existence proofs of undisclosed value influence in these testbeds, state where the setups are artificial, and avoid positioning it as a distinct category of misalignment or as a gap in current evaluations.

=== key bc2a84d4dd92
Context: A team of authors was writing up a threat they call secret loyalties, where an AI covertly advances a particular person's or group's interests. Only a small amount of prior empirical work existed: narrow trigger-based models had been built, and black-box auditing and interrogation of them had mostly failed. The authors had audited existing defenses (data monitoring, behavioral evaluations, interpretability, runtime monitoring) and needed to decide how to organize the research they recommended to the field.
O1: Run and publish one deep empirical study that builds loyal models and tests a few detection methods, with no broader agenda, to understand how loyalties form even if no defensive decision depends on it yet.
O2: Frame the topic as one item inside a broader control agenda on covertly poisoning other AI systems, with general-science questions such as how much data is needed to instill coherent loyalties and how hard they are to detect.
O3: Build one reproducible testbed where loyalty is installed in realistic, documents-delivered contexts with matched controls and ablations, and report how detection depends on whether the model can recognise it is being tested.
O4: Pick a single checkable endpoint, such as an auditor finding a loyalty-driven action within a long mundane agentic trajectory against a best-responding attacker, and scope all claims to what that one validated setup shows.
O5: The document proposes a five-direction research agenda outlining concrete lines of inquiry to pursue.
